newsitem.title: USA: Albright's trip lifts expectations on Bosnia peace.
newsitem.headline: Albright's trip lifts expectations on Bosnia peace.

text.p: With the force of her personality and will, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has imbued the U.S.-led international peace effort in Bosnia with a new energy, raising expectations for success.
The strategy is risky but so was limping along and letting the Bosnian peace process deteriorate -- as it had in recent months.

The issue now is whether Washington and its international partners have the political will to implement the strategy over the long term -- especially if it means keeping NATO-led troops in the region beyond a deadline of June 1998 or taking extraordinary action to seize war criminals.
During two days of intensive activity in the Balkans last weekend, Albright butted heads with key regional leaders.
Seldom has Washington gone so public with such withering criticism of parties to a major peace deal, in this case the 1995 U.S.-brokered Dayton accord ending the Bosnia war.
"She spoke in the language of the region," one U.S. official said of the area that has more than its share of bullies. "Diplomatic niceties just don't work out here."

A former refugee from Czechoslovakia who lived in Belgrade as a child, she exploited some of her most celebrated traits -- distilling complex issues into simple terms and using the media to send diplomatic messages with practiced soundbites.

With Croatian President Franjo Tudjman in Zagreb and later on Serbian President Slobodan Milozevic's home turf of Belgrade, Albright excoriated the two men for not living up to their Dayton vows on refugees, war criminals and other issues.
The next day in Bosnia, she told Serb republic leaders they had the worst record on war criminals and pledged that indicted suspects would ultimately be brought to trial in the Hague.

The sense of risk to her personal safety was palpable. Presiding at a bridge-opening in Brcko, site of some of the Bosnia war's most brutal violence, she wore a bullet-proof vest, her security agents openly carried Uzi machine guns and U.S. helicopters kept an eye on nearby woods for snipers.
More than just tough words, Albright also carried a hammer: a promise Washington would tie bilateral aid and other benefits to the leaders' meeting Dayton commitments and other U.S. demands.
Her hard line reflects a major conclusion of a U.S. review of Bosnia policy that "everything has to be linked," U.S. official said.
The U.S. position was bolstered by action in Portugal last Friday with France, Germany, Russia and Britain. All insisted they would "not tolerate a resumption of hostilities by anyone" in Bosnia.
Adding credibility to what is often only rhetoric, the communique threated penalties on Bosnia's Moslem, Croat and Serb factions if certain Dayton accord demands are not met.
Among these would be denying economic aid to Bosnian Serb towns that "tolerate" indicted war criminals working in the government and that do not allow refugees to return home.
But the international threats are geared to Bosnian groups and do not target Serbia and Croatia, who also signed the Bosnia peace deal and whose adherence is vital to its success.

While the world may concur in holding Bosnia factions accountable, there is less stomach for punishing Serbia and Croatia, with their historical ties to major states. U.S. officials say the European Union cares more about commercial deals with Zagreb and Belgrade.

The international war crimes tribunal at the Hague has indicted 75 suspects from Bosnia. So for only nine have been arrested and this inability to bring suspects to justice is viewed as a major threat to peace in Bosnia.

Despite the U.S. push, international envoy to Bosnia Carl Bildt doubts economic sanctions will be enough to persuade Balkan leaders to deliver war criminals to the Hague. At some point, military force will be needed, he said.

Washington has explored creating a special military unit to track down war criminals. It is unclear where the proposal stands but Albright insisted repeatedly "we will do everything we can to support the war crimes tribunal more actively."

Her trip proved she has won the day, for now, on a more hawkish U.S. line on the Balkans. Defence Secretary William Cohen two months ago declared that U.S. troops would pull out of Bosnia in June 1998 whether or not a new war erupted.

Albright has reasserted a sustained U.S. commitment. And while making clear he has no plans to keep American troops in Bosnia beyond the target date, President Bill Clinton last week left open the possibility this could change.
